10.0.0.en: 1 A wise judge will instruct his people; and the government of a prudent man is well ordered. 2 As the judge of the people is himself, so are his officers; and what manner of man the ruler of the city is, such are all they that dwell therein. 3 An unwise king destroyeth his people; but through the prudence of them which are in authority the city shall be inhabited.

10.0.1.en: The wise leader teaches his people, and the government of a prudent man is well ordered [1].

10.0.2.en: God created man to be a leader of himself before he leads others, and whenever he assumes a position of leadership, whether on the family, social, military, or religious level, he must all the more adorn himself with wisdom, for he becomes responsible for those under his leadership, and he becomes a model for them, which they follow.

10.0.3.en: What occupies Ben Sira's mind concerning the ruler or the heads of cities is not merely their political, economic, or recreational administration, etc., but rather concern for the peace of the people and their building up, so that a generation with a sound character may arise. The successful leader raises up, if possible, from all his people leaders who realize their mission and their role in a spirit of moderation and joy.

10.0.4.en: The wonderful example in the history of Israel is King Solomon the Wise, who by his broad mind and wise leadership drew even the kings around him to learn from him. For example, the queen of Sheba came to prove him with hard questions (1 Kgs 10:1), and it was said of her: "And when the queen of Sheba had seen all Solomon's wisdom, and the house that he had built, and the meat of his table, and the sitting of his servants, and the attendance of his ministers, and their apparel, and his cupbearers, and his burnt offerings... there was no more spirit in her" (1 Kgs 10:4-5). She said: "Happy are thy men, happy are these thy servants, which stand continually before thee, and that hear thy wisdom" (1 Kgs 10:8).

10.0.5.en: But the wicked kings destroyed themselves and drew woes upon the people, for from the time of Rehoboam son of Solomon the kingdom was divided into two kingdoms, the separated kingdom of Israel and the kingdom of Judah, that is, the northern kingdom and the southern kingdom, and often one of them joined foreign nations to resist its sister. The first fell under the captivity of Assyria and the second under the Babylonian captivity, and idolatry entered both kingdoms, even into the temple of the Lord in Jerusalem.

10.1.0.en: As the leader of the people behaves, so do his ministers, and all the inhabitants of the city are the mirror of their ruler [2].

10.1.1.en: The leader is a teacher to those around him and those under his authority. He teaches not by words but rather by his management and conduct. His role does not consist only in the good management of affairs, but he leads them in godliness, especially in the fear of the Lord. Perhaps the greatest example in the Old Testament is David's stand when his military companions asked him to kill King Saul, who was pursuing him and had fallen into his hands; he gave them a practical lesson in not taking vengeance on him who had devoted his royal powers to killing him (1 Sam 24:1-8).

10.1.2.en: St. John Chrysostom stands in amazement, asking in his depths: Was pious David a commander of a battle, or a teacher, or a priest or a bishop? He sees him as the good teacher, careful that neither he nor any of his men should stretch out a hand to evil. The soldiers accompanied David to protect him from the plots of Saul and his attempts to kill him, and he accompanied them to protect them from any unholy action or thought. He cares for the salvation of his own soul as for theirs.

10.1.3.en: He sees him also as the priest or the bishop, for wherever pious David was, he considered himself in the presence of the Lord, as one in a holy temple. The cave was in his eyes a holy church in which he practiced the work of teaching; he spoke with his companions as with Saul to guide them to the way of their salvation. He preached the truth and was careful for the salvation of all.

10.1.4.en: Chrysostom sees him as like a bishop or priest offering the sacrifice of love and the offering of meekness and mercy. He also sees him as like a ransom, offering his life poured out by his pardon of his opponent who sought his soul, and he sees the cave as like a holy altar and a temple of the Lord, which does not allow any unseemly thought to have a place in it [1].

10.1.5.en: v You see that it was not possible without the work of God that (David) should succeed in mastering these men of great fury; the grace of God was found on the lips of the inspired man, offering a kind of these persuasive words. In any case David's contribution was not small, for he had formed them in the past, and therefore found them in the decisive moment ready and willing (in what they had learned from him). You see that he was not like a commander of troops (an army) giving them orders, but like a priest, and the cave was a church on this occasion.

10.1.6.en: He was like one consecrated a bishop giving them a homily. And after the homily he offered a kind of wonderful, extraordinary sacrifice, not by offering a bull as a sacrifice nor by slaying a lamb, but something greater than both: he offered to God meekness and mercy, slaying the (hidden) rage that did not work in him, killing anger, and putting to death the members which are upon the earth. He acted as ransom and priest and altar. Everything came forth from him, the thought which offered kindness and mercy, and meekness of heart, the things which he made offerings (to God) [2].

10.1.7.en: v Let no one say: I have a wicked, corrupt, and stubborn enemy, who arouses disgust. Whatever you say about him, there is none more wicked than Saul, whom David rescued on many occasions, who personally devised countless plots, and yet David offered him kindnesses in return for his evils, while he persisted in his evil. What plea do you present after this? Have they seized part of your land, have they broken into your possessions, and trespassed on the borders of your house, and stolen your servants, and harmed you, and been greedy, and brought you down to poverty? Yet they did not take your life, which was what that man (Saul) was determined upon. And if they were determined to take your life, perhaps they tried this on one occasion, not time after time like him. And if they repeated it several times, still they did not receive such benefits from you, for they did not fall into your hands once or twice and you spared them. And if this happened, David is still more generous.

10.1.8.en: It was impossible for a man under the economy of the Old Testament to attain deep values, but now, after the coming of grace, such wonderful excellences have been given. David had not heard of the parable of the ten thousand talents and the hundred denarii (Mt 18:23-30). Nor did he hear the prayer which says: "Forgive them what they owe, as your heavenly Father forgives you" (see Mt 6:14). He did not see Christ crucified, nor the precious blood flowing, nor did he hear the countless words about sound values. He did not benefit from the countless blessings of sound values. He did not benefit from the blessings of the wonderful sacrifice, nor partake of the blood of the Lord. Instead he was brought up under the imperfect laws which did not require these things, and yet he attained the summit of the sound values of the age of grace.

10.1.9.en: While you are often offended by past injuries and murmur, he on the contrary, with fear of what would happen in the future, and with full awareness that if he saved the man's life the city would lose its immunity as far as he was concerned and his own life would perish, yet did not cease to show care (for his enemy). He did all in his power to protect him who bore him enmity. Who could have acquired greater patience than this?

10.1.10.en: As for you, learn also from what happened in our days. In any case, we can be reconciled with every person who bears enmity toward us if we wish. What can be fiercer than the lion, and yet men tame it. For skillful training brings out what is better in nature, and the fiercest animal, which is reckoned a king, becomes gentler than a flock of sheep, and moves about in the marketplaces without causing terror to anyone. What excuse then do we have? What plea do we have if wild beasts are tamed, if we claim that human beings cannot be calmed or drawn to take a friendly attitude toward us?

10.1.11.en: In truth fierceness in animals is due to nature, but in the human being it is against nature, so if we overcome nature, what excuse do we have when we claim that free will cannot be reformed?... Let us concentrate on one thing, not on our not suffering the harm that comes to us from our enemies, but on making them unable to harm our souls. For we are not troubled even if they measure out to us troubles without number. David suffered nothing, though he was driven out and became a wanderer, and was the object of plots to end his life; instead he became all the more famous and revered more than the other (Saul), and became all the more beloved by everyone, not by men only, but by God Himself. Above all this, what harm came to the saint from enduring all this from Saul at that time? Are his psalms not sung to this day? Did he not become famous on earth and still more in heaven? Do not indescribable good things await him, even in the Kingdom of Heaven?

10.2.0.en: And on the other side, what good did this wretched, miserable man gain by his terrible plots? Did he not lose his royal position, and a pitiable death befell him and his son, and he fell under accusations directed at him by all, and what is worse than this, the eternal punishment awaits him which he will meet? [3]

10.2.1.en: St. John Chrysostom: An unrestrained king destroys his people, but through the wisdom of its rulers a city becomes habitable [3].

10.2.2.en: We saw King David rescuing his men from falling into vengeance on King Saul (1 Sam 24:6-7), while King Saul with his corrupt heart spread corruption among those around him.

10.3.s.en: 2. The Lord, giver of wisdom to the administrator

10.3.0.en: 4 The kingdom of the earth is in the hand of the Lord, and in due time he setteth over it one that is profitable. 5 The success of man is in the hand of the Lord, and upon the face of the scribe he layeth his honour. 6 If thy neighbour wrong thee in any thing, be not wroth with him, and do nothing of the things of insult.

10.3.1.en: The kingdom of the earth is in the hand of the Lord, and He sets over it the fitting man at the fitting time [4].

10.3.2.en: Ben Sira affirms the Lord's care for all nations and peoples, so kings and rulers are not set up in random ways, but with God's permission for good. A people careless of their salvation and resisting the truth, God permits them to choose an evil leader, that they may realize that what befell them is the fruit of their evil, that perhaps they may repent of corruption and injustice. When the evil of the Babylonians increased and they thought that there was no power in the world that could, now or in the future, stand before them, He permitted Belshazzar, the grandson of Nebuchadnezzar, probably his daughter's son, who did not benefit from the lessons of his fathers, to reign over them (Dan 5). Belshazzar defied God Himself and deliberately wished to insult Him. As St. Jerome says: [He was not sober when he did these things, but rather was drunk, forgetting the punishment that befell his predecessor Nebuchadnezzar [4].]

10.3.3.en: Belshazzar was occupied with holding a banquet for a thousand of the great men who came from every place, with his wives and concubines. He thought it impossible for Cyrus or anyone else to breach the walls of the huge city, so he let him besiege it, in contempt of him and his army. The walls of Babylon, as Herodotus reports, were no less than 87 feet in width and 350 feet in height, with 250 towers rising another 100 feet in the air. Therefore Belshazzar thought that no one could invade Babylon.

10.3.4.en: The effort Belshazzar made in holding the banquet and the resources that were provided cannot be estimated. And this in defiance of God, for instead of fasting during the time of the siege and crying out to God to save him and his city, he held a banquet, and used the holy vessels for drinking to defile them in an atmosphere of corruption and licentiousness. And while Belshazzar was opening the banquet, the army of Cyrus was at the gates of Babylon. Cyrus had diverted many channels of the Euphrates and suddenly broke into the city, and the kingdom of Babylon came to an end. Belshazzar was responsible for those under his command, and they, together with the rest of the people, were for their part wicked, for God often permits the discipline of a people through the setting up of a wicked leader. And God has often changed the hearts and thoughts of wicked leaders through the prayers of the subordinates and their fear of the Lord and their holy conduct.

10.4.0.en: The success of man is in the hand of the Lord, and He gives his glory to the person of the scribe [5].

10.4.1.en: God in His justice gives success to those who strive, and raises up from among them great leaders. Some see that the word "scribe" here means the decision maker, or the ruler. The class of scribes among the Jews was educated, copying the Holy Scriptures and interpreting them and teaching by them. In the days of the Lord Christ they were looked upon as an exalted class, and many of the priests in Jerusalem served as scribes. They joined special schools and studied particular curricula. Among them were the Jewish historian Josephus, and also Hillel, who was a scholar and became a famous teacher.

10.5.0.en: 7 Pride is hateful before the Lord and men, and its way is the committing of iniquity before both. 8 But the kingdom is transferred from nation to nation because of injustices and insults and riches. 9 No one is more hideous in guilt than the miser. Why is dust and ashes proud? 10 No one is greater in iniquity than he that loveth money, for he maketh his own soul also a thing for sale, and hath cast away his bowels during his life. 11 Every authority is short-lived. A long sickness is a burden to the physician. 12 So the physician cuts off the sickness before it lengthens; thus the king reigns today and tomorrow he dies. 13 And man at his death inheriteth vipers and beasts and worms. 14 The beginning of man's pride is his departing from the Lord, 15 when his heart turneth away from his Maker. For pride is the beginning of sin, and he in whom it is rooted overflows with abominations. 16 And therefore the Lord brought upon them that have it strange calamities, and destroyed them utterly.

10.5.1.en: Be not wroth with thy neighbour for any harm he has caused, and do not practice any of the acts of insult [6].

10.5.2.en: Ben Sira learned from the conduct of David the prophet, who did not allow even his men to stretch out their hands in evil against Saul.

10.5.3.en: When David was vexed with Nabal who insulted him and gave him nothing to eat, him and his young men who had guarded his possessions and his sheep, he drew his sword, and with him about four hundred men with drawn swords, to fight him. The Lord sent him Abigail, Nabal's wise wife, to turn him back from this deed with wisdom and dignity. She fell at his feet, and said: "That this shall be no grief unto thee, nor offence of heart unto my lord, that thou hast shed blood causeless, or that my lord hath avenged himself." David answered her: "And blessed be thy advice, and blessed be thou, which hast kept me this day from coming to shed blood, and from avenging myself with mine own hand" (1 Sam 25:33).

10.5.4.en: Ben Sira warns us against making any decision when a man is stirred up and agitated. Malice, hatred, and wrath are among the fruits of pride. The humble man has compassion on every person, even him who wrongs him (Lev 19:17-18).

10.5.5.en: v The (believer) must not be angry with his neighbor without cause, nor adopt resentment against anyone, nor repay evil with evil. It is fitting for him to be reviled rather than to revile, to be struck rather than to strike, to be wronged rather than to sin, and to be robbed rather than to rob [5].

10.5.6.en: v Anger makes tongues unbridled, and talk without restraint. Likewise physical violence and acts of mockery, abuse, accusations, beating and other countless evil deeds are born of anger and resentment [6].

10.5.7.en: v Hateful and ugly is that soul which has given itself to its passions. Who can look at a man in his anger and his ugly form? And who can look at a sorrowful man, feeble before his own enslaved soul?...

10.5.8.en: Let us then be careful of our beauty, so that the Bridegroom, the Word, may receive us with welcome with these words: "Thou art all fair, my love; there is no spot in thee" (Song 4:7) [7].

10.6.0.en: v The chaste in the desire for honor is humble. The chaste in riches is content, and attains the measure of the Gospel in poverty. He who controls resentment and anger is gentle. In truth the observance of true chastity governs the tongue and sets a limit for the eyes and cleanses the ears from listening to gossip with curiosity. But he who does not keep all this is not chaste but unruly [8].

10.6.1.en: St. Basil the Great: St. Pachomius says that he who teaches the wrathful to become meek has cast a demon out of him.

10.6.2.en: Haughtiness is hateful before the Lord and men, and injustice is shameful to both [7].

10.6.3.en: The haughtiness of the ruler drives the nation to collapse. Examples of this are what befell Egypt of plagues in the days of Moses because of the pride of Pharaoh (Ex 7-11). Ben Sira learned this lesson from the fall of Assyria (612 BC) and the kingdom of Babylon (539 BC) and Persia (331 BC) and Greece (323 BC), etc.

10.6.4.en: v O distinguished one, do not exalt yourself over your neighbor; humble yourself before him, and if possible fall before his feet.

10.6.5.en: Picture before your eyes the humility of the Son of God, and as He humbled Himself, humble yourself also to your equals.

10.6.6.en: Look at Him humbled as He washes the feet of the members of His household, and being God, He loved humility and hated boasting.

10.6.7.en: What the Son of God hates, do not approach, for if you approach it, it will kill you and corrupt you.

10.6.8.en: Hate the pride which the Son of God hated and rejected: it is the evil from which all evils spring.

10.6.9.en: Love humility, and hate boasting; if you are a disciple, all the demons cannot approach you.

10.6.10.en: Humility cast them down from their ranks, and if they find humility in you they flee from you.

10.6.11.en: Humility is the house of divinity, and where it is, God dwells in it...

10.6.12.en: Be humble that the King may come and dwell with you, and all the power of the enemy will not harm you.

10.6.13.en: The house of the king is not plundered by thieves, because his soldiers guard its gates with care.

10.6.14.en: If you are humble, behold the Kingdom dwells in you, and neither robbers nor thieves will rob you.

10.7.0.en: If you are humble, the tree of all evil is plucked out of you, and our Lord plants in its place the blessed Tree [9].

10.7.1.en: St. Jacob of Serugh: The kingdom is transferred from nation to nation because of injustice, arrogance, and money [8].

10.7.2.en: Nothing corrupts any kingdom, state, or family like injustice, arrogance, and the love of money.

10.8.0.en: v We read, beloved dear ones, in the Holy Bible: "Blessed is the rich man who does not run after gain... he could transgress and did not transgress, and do evil and did not do it" (see Sir 10:8-10). Well, brethren, let us ask our consciences and see whether we despise covetousness in a way by which we share in this blessing [10].

10.8.1.en: Father Caesarius, bishop of Arles: How can he who is dust and ashes be proud?

10.8.2.en: For even during his lifetime his bowels stink? [9]

10.8.3.en: Ben Sira stands amazed at man, created of dust and ashes, for while he is still in this life, as he is occupied with earthly things instead of his inner life, his depths become corrupt and foul!

10.8.4.en: v The man who turns toward outward things changes into what is worse, and while alive he casts out his bowels (see Sir 10:9). By this he appears to the world to be in a better state, to those who think on earthly things (Phil 3:19), when the sinner is praised for the desires of his soul and the unjust man is called blessed.

10.9.0.en: v He changes for the better when his interest gradually turns away from the earthly things that appear in this world, and he places his glory in the inward things on high [11].

10.9.1.en: St. Augustine: It is wonderful that man, while remaining dust and ashes, is proud even toward his Creator, and when he is united with the Most High he becomes heaven and is humble, imitating the Lord Christ who says: "Learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart."

10.9.2.en: St. Augustine says that if the devil has no justification for his pride, though he is not dust and ashes, then how will man justify his pride? It is wonderful that when man casts off his (foul) inward parts, the reaction is not contrition and humility but covering himself with pride and arrogance.

10.9.3.en: v It is said: "There went up a spring from the earth and watered the whole face of the earth" (Gen 2:6). It went up from that land of which Scripture said: "Thou art my hope, my portion in the land of the living" (Ps 142:6). When the soul was watered by such a spring it had not yet thirsted for its inner depths by pride. For the beginning of man's pride is the departing from God (see Sir 10:12). And when it is puffed up by outward things through pride, the soul ceases to be watered by the inner spring. Therefore we are rightly mocked by the words of the prophet who says: "Why is he proud who is dust and ashes, and whose bowels have stunk during his life?" (see Sir 10:9).

10.10.0.en: From the Fathers of the Iberian Peninsula v "For what man knoweth the things of a man, save the spirit of man which is in him?" (1 Cor 2:11). And yet there are things of man which the spirit that is in him does not know. But You, O Lord, who made him, know him completely. In truth, though I am the object of Your sight, I despise myself and count myself nothing but dust and ashes. I know something that is Yours, and I do not know myself. Surely we see in a dark mirror "and not face to face" (1 Cor 13:12). As long as I am far from You I am nearer to myself than I am to You [12].

10.10.1.en: v I tremble, for the cause of the soul's estrangement from God is that it is proud. I do not doubt this. It is written: "Pride is the beginning of sin" (see Sir 10:13), and the beginning of human pride is distance from God. It is written that this is firm and true. And so what was said of the pride of transient humanity, wrapped in the worn-out rags of the flesh, weighed down by the corruptible body (Wis 9:15), and for a while man exalts himself, forgetting what the very skin is which he wears. Why does he exalt himself? Let the Holy Scriptures tell us: "Because his bowels have stunk" [9]... The proud man gets rid of his bowels, but the humble man longs zealously for his depths. If by pride we are driven out, by humility we return [13].

10.10.2.en: St. Augustine v Someone may say: How can he who falls into the sin of frivolity acquire the devil in his soul? What we say, beloved dear ones, we prove from the Holy Scriptures.

10.10.3.en: Listen to Holy Scripture, which says that the proud man is full of the devil: "Every one that is proud in heart is an abomination to the LORD" (see Prov 16:5), and "Every pride is the beginning of departing from God" (see Sir 10:12). What does departing from God mean but separating from Him? Moreover, the man who withdraws from God necessarily unites with the devil. Scripture also says that the envious man cannot be without the devil. "Through envy of the devil death entered into the world and they that follow him take his side." The prophet says: "The spirit of whoredoms hath caused them to err" (Hos 4:12).

10.11.0.en: Father Caesarius, bishop of Arles v Pride, haughtiness, and arrogance are the sins of Satan, and because of these faults he left heaven for earth [Satan fell from heaven]. Therefore "God resisteth the proud, and giveth grace to the humble" (Jas 4:6). For he who is arrogant forgets what he will become, what frailty will befall him, and in what filth he will sink, and what dung heap continually comes out of his body. What do the divine Scriptures say? How can he who was made of dust and ashes boast? By the corruption of man's inward parts. Pride is the most dangerous of all sins, the chief fault of Satan [14].

10.12.0.en: All rational creation in the heavens and on earth is in need of the divine grace which binds it to God, so that it does not fall into pride, and consequently does not isolate itself from Him as the source of its goodness. When one of the heavenly orders isolated itself from God by accepting pride, it was deprived of divine grace and became powers of darkness, unable to bear the light. And likewise when our first parents rejected grace and clung to the promises and guidance of the devil, they fell into pride. He who departs from God or isolates himself from Him perishes, for he walks according to his own evil will, not according to the holy will of God.

10.12.1.en: Fulgentius, disciple of St. Augustine, sees that the first man was in need of divine grace.

10.12.2.en: v In truth human nature could not by its own power achieve this possibility, that is, doing good, even for the first man before he was wounded by sin. Therefore, how could man regain his health without the help of the physician, if while in health he was not able to succeed in guarding his health at that time? For this reason dust and ashes ought not to boast, because deep thought in this life has forsaken it (Sir 10:9), and it was not possible for the wounded to act as one in full health, counting that his wound had been healed. Rather he needed in humility to reveal his wounded heart and the stench of his wounds. So he declares with the prophet: "My wounds stink and are corrupt because of my foolishness" (Ps 38:5), and he is able to receive healing not by his merit, but through the gift of free divine mercy. In truth how can man possess what he has not received? And since he has received it, why does he glory as if he had not received it (see 1 Cor 4:7)? [15]

10.12.3.en: v Man began to sin through isolating himself from God. It is written: "The beginning of pride is departing from God" (see Sir 10:14), and in another place: "For, lo, they that are far from thee shall perish: thou hast destroyed all them that go a whoring from thee" (Ps 73:27). Those who depart from God and commit adultery perish... God does not wish their destruction by His judgment unless they destroy themselves by their iniquities [16].

10.12.4.en: Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe v Let the humble listen to the voice of the royal Truth: "He that humbleth himself shall be exalted," and let the proud know that "every one that exalteth himself shall be abased" (Lk 18:14). Let the humble know that "before honour is humility" (Prov 15:33), and let the proud know that "before destruction is pride" (Prov 16:18). Let the humble know that: "To this man will I look, even to him that is poor and of a contrite spirit, and trembleth at my word" (Isa 66:2), and let the proud remember the saying: "Why is dust and ashes proud?" (see Sir 10:9). Let the humble know that "The Lord is high, yet hath he respect unto the lowly," and of the proud He says: "But the proud he knoweth afar off" (Ps 138:6). Let the humble know that: "The Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister" (Mt 20:28), and let the proud know that "Pride is the beginning of sin (and he in whom it is rooted overflows with abominations)" (see Sir 10:15). Let the humble know that our Savior: "humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross" (Phil 2:8).

10.12.5.en: Let the proud know what is written of their chief: "When he raiseth up himself, the mighty are afraid" "he is a king over all the children of pride" (Job 41:25, 34). By the pride of the devil judgment came upon us, and by the humility of God the covenant of our salvation was accomplished. For our enemy, a creature like all creatures, wished to exalt himself above all, but our Savior deemed it right to become small among all, and thus remained exalted and great above all. Therefore let the meek know that they are raised up to be like God when they humble themselves. And let the lofty know that by their conceit they descend to the likeness of the rebel angel. There is nothing lower than the conceit that casts man down from the state of true exaltation. And how exalted is humility which, by descending to the depths, is joined to the Creator who is above all in the heights [17].

10.12.7.en: A chronic illness puzzles the physician, and the king of today dies tomorrow [10].

10.12.8.en: When a man dies he inherits creeping things, beasts, and worms [11].

10.12.9.en: The beginning of man's pride is his departing from the Lord, for his heart withdraws from his Maker [12].

10.12.10.en: v The children of God and the children of the devil are not distinguished from each other except through humility and pride. When you see a proud man do not doubt that he is a son of the devil. And if you see a humble man you must believe and trust that he is a son of God... What cast down the devil but pride, and what raised Christ is humility, for He set the healing of humility for the wound of pride. Therefore if we wish to avoid pride we must always withdraw into the medicine of humility. Let us listen to the Lord who says: "Learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart" (Mt 11:29). He did not say learn of me the creation of the world, or the raising of the dead or the working of other miracles.

10.13.0.en: Father Caesarius, bishop of Arles v He who is proud suffers the same punishment as the devil, because: the beginning of man's pride is his departing from the Lord (see Sir 10:12). Pride is the beginning of sin, and it is the first impulse and movement toward evil. In truth perhaps it is both the root and the foundation. For the beginning means the first impulse toward evil or the background of evil. It is like a person saying that the beginning of purity is abstaining from looking at unseemly things, for this is the impulse. But to say that the beginning of purity is fasting, this is the foundation which establishes purity. So pride is the beginning of sin, because every sin begins with it and it supports it [18].

10.14.0.en: v Had Satan not been struck by this disease (arrogance) he would not have descended and become Satan, for he was not formerly Satan. This is what cast him from that confidence, this drove him into the pit of fire, this is the cause of all his woes [19].

10.14.1.en: St. John Chrysostom v The beginning of human sin is rebellion against God, and the beginning of every sin is pride. The Apostle spoke of this matter concerning sin, saying: "Because that, when they knew God, they glorified him not as God, neither were thankful; but became vain in their imaginations, and their foolish heart was darkened" (Rom 1:21). The darkened heart has its punishment in itself. But from where did this happen? "Professing themselves to be wise, they became fools" (Rom 1:22). They said that what they received from God came from themselves. Or even if they knew from whom they received this, they did not give glory to him from whom they received.

10.14.2.en: v Misery is the seeds of iniquity, but sin is the conception of misery; for the first sin is departing from God [12]. He who conceives misery travails with injustice. Iniquity itself is like injustice, it brings forth that with which it has travailed [20].

10.14.3.en: St. Augustine: For the beginning of man's pride is sin, and he who holds to it overflows with abomination.

10.14.4.en: And therefore the Lord brings upon the proud exceeding trials, and destroys them utterly [13].

10.14.5.en: It is not necessarily so that every sin is accompanied by pride, but every sin has as its first cause pride and man's isolating himself from his God, and his rejecting the divine will.

10.15.0.en: v He who has learned well the steps of overcoming vices knows that this vice of vainglory must be avoided entirely... for that by which the soul first fell rules the rest. "For the beginning of all sin is pride," and also: "The beginning of man's pride is his departing from God" (see Sir 10:12-13) [21].

10.16.0.en: v When the soul loves its own authority it descends from what is common to all to what is its own. Had it followed God as its leader in the universal creation, His laws could keep it at the highest level of exaltation [22].

10.17.0.en: v Blessedness needs nothing else whatever, since it needs to attain the highest wisdom. "But the fear of the Lord is the head of wisdom" (Ps 111:10) LXX. On the other hand pride is called "the beginning of all sin" (see Sir 10:13). The proud man seeks the love of earthly kingdoms, but "Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven" (Mt 5:3) [23].

10.18.0.en: St. Augustine v I beseech you that we be zealous to turn away from this inclination (pride), lest we fall into the same condemnation, and submit ourselves to the same punishment, and share in the vengeance. He says: "Not a novice, lest being lifted up with pride he fall into the condemnation of the devil" (1 Tim 3:6). He who is puffed up suffers the same punishment as the devil. "The beginning of pride is not knowing the Lord" (see Sir 10:12) [24].

10.19.0.en: v A wise man says: "Pride is the beginning of sin" (see Sir 10:13), that is, its root, its source, and its mother [25].

10.20.0.en: v In truth there is nothing so alien to the mercy of God, and casts into the fire of Gehenna like the tyrant of pride. If we possess it within us, our life becomes defiled, even if we practice purity and virginity and fasting and prayer and almsgiving or any virtue whatsoever. Scripture says: "Every one that is proud in heart is an abomination to the LORD" (Prov 16:5). Therefore we must press down this haughtiness of the soul, and cut off this tumor, if we wish to be pure and be rid of the punishment prepared for the devil [26].

10.21.s.en: 4. The greatness of the meek is the fear of the Lord

10.21.0.en: 17 The Lord hath overthrown the thrones of the sultans, and set the meek in their place. 18 The Lord hath plucked up the roots of the nations, and planted the humble in their place. 19 The Lord overturned the lands of the nations, and destroyed them to the foundations of the earth. 20 He made some of them dry, and destroyed their inhabitants, and removed their memorial from the earth. 21 The Lord blotted out the memorial of the proud, and left the memorial of them that are humble in spirit. 22 Pride was not created with men, nor wrath with them that are born of women.

10.21.1.en: The Lord destroys the thrones of the sultans, and seats the meek in their place [14].

10.21.2.en: The Apostle says: "And that he died for all, that they which live should henceforth not live unto themselves, but unto him which died for them, and rose again" (2 Cor 5:15). The statement here is an echo of what is stated in (Prov 3:35) and in (1 Pet 5:5-6).

10.21.3.en: v Our Christ came to reconcile us with God (the Father) by His humility, since we had strayed from Him by our accursed pride...

10.22.0.en: "Pride is the beginning of all sins." Likewise we read: "The first of man's pride is the fall by departing from the Lord" (see Sir 10:13-14). Therefore may no one live for himself but for Christ, and do His will, and not the will of man himself, and abide in His love, and do the will of his Father and dwell in His love (Jn 15:10) [27].

10.23.0.en: St. Augustine v Is there another proud man? Let him hear: "God resisteth the proud" (Jas 4:6). And "Pride is the first beginning of sin" (see Sir 10:13). "Every one that is proud in heart is an abomination to the LORD" (Prov 16:5) [28].

10.23.1.en: St. John Chrysostom: St. Jacob of Serugh presents us with a wonderful picture of the pagan king of Nineveh as he saves his kingdom by his faith with a spirit of humility and repentance. 1. In humility, he did not despise a man without weapons (Jonah), poor and appearing in his looks as lowly. 2. He left the royal throne, offering repentance in contrition and sincere repentance. 3. He gathered the people so that all might take part, even the little children, in the battle. 4. He realized that the weapon of the infants and children is greater and stronger than every weapon, for by them they win the battle, and seize the great mercies of God.

10.23.2.en: St. Jacob of Serugh depicts for us the meeting of Jonah the prophet with the king of Nineveh, saying:

10.23.3.en: v Jonah said: There is no means of averting the wrath, for iniquity has grown strong and the overthrow has come to shatter you.

10.23.4.en: Evil is decreed and the appointed end has arrived; affliction has drawn near, and the fall is at the door.

10.23.5.en: The Lord sent me, that Mighty One who bears creation, to proclaim the overthrow, and with a cry of terror upon your walls.

10.23.6.en: That Strong One who by His command terrified all creatures, and looks upon the earth, and it trembles before Him because He is its Lord.

10.23.7.en: He who disciplined the earth with the waters of retribution and destroyed the sinners from it and they did not escape.

10.23.8.en: He who scattered the peoples in the regions from the days of Babel, and when they sinned against Him confused their tongues and destroyed them...

10.23.9.en: These voices struck the king of Nineveh, and he was terrified when he heard the fearful tidings.

10.23.10.en: He feared Jonah more than thousands of mighty men, and the king fell before that lowly man.

10.23.11.en: He rose from his splendid throne, and cast the crown from him, and put on sackcloth, and prepared himself for repentance.

10.23.12.en: He saw that Jonah did not wish to retract what he said, so he thought to nullify his words by contradictions.

10.23.13.en: He found that the prophet threatened much and strongly, so he girded up his loins (resolved his matter) to face the danger with might.

10.23.14.en: He knew what that battle required, so he prepared himself to set up the front like a valiant man.

10.23.15.en: He realized that this battle was not like the usual battles, so he gathered his people and urged them to strive.

10.23.16.en: He gathered his soldiers and drew them up for supplication, and supplied the ranks of the soldiers with prayers to close the gaps.

10.23.17.en: He made men and women and children hold to fasting, each according to his strength, to line up for the fight against the wrath.

10.23.18.en: The king said to his soldiers such words as these to his armies gathered together for the supplication.

10.23.19.en: A new fight we are entering, unfamiliar. Let us awaken our souls to victory by virtue.

10.23.20.en: Lay down the weapons, and take sackcloth instead of armor, and leave the arrows, and let the voice of supplications pour forth from us.

10.23.21.en: Let the children and the elders arise and line up against the wrath, and let men and women fight against destruction.

10.23.22.en: And let not even a one-day-old be kept from the battle, for the fight is fierce, so let us not show weariness in it.

10.23.23.en: A boy who has not sinned defeats a thousand in this battle; let them come with us, for the whole war is won by them.

10.23.24.en: Behold the Hebrew threatens and waves to destroy us; let us confront him lest he rejoice over us when he overcomes us.

10.23.25.en: Infants at the breast take part with us here among the ranks and support us, until evil is driven back from us.

10.23.26.en: In this fight the boys are stronger than the men, and the children strive more easily than the mighty.

10.24.0.en: The children who have not sinned defeat thousands in this battle, and take part with us, and through them the struggle becomes better [29].

10.24.1.en: St. Jacob of Serugh: The Lord plucks up the roots of the nations, and plants the humble in their place [15].

10.24.2.en: When a believing man dies we feel that his memory lasts forever, because he is in the presence of God, but the wicked, whether on the level of individuals or nations, end as though they had never existed before.

10.25.0.en: v It is customary to say of the proud man that he has lofty spirits. And this is true, because the wind is called spirit. And so it is written: "Fire, and hail; snow, and vapour; stormy wind (Spirit of tempest)" (Ps 148:8). Indeed the proud man is called puffed up, as if he were exalted with the wind. And here the Apostle says: "Knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth" (1 Cor 8:1)... Let us understand in truth that the poor in spirit are the humble and those who fear God, that is, those who do not have the spirit that is puffed up. In truth the Beatitudes could not begin with anything other than this beginning, since they are set for the attainment of the high wisdom "the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom" (Ps 111:10), and on the other hand "Pride is the beginning of sins" (see Sir 10:5). Then let the proud man seek and love earthly kingdoms, but "Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven" [30].

10.25.1.en: St. Augustine: The Lord overturns the lands of the nations, and destroys them to the foundations of the earth [16].

10.25.2.en: He shakes some of them, and destroys their inhabitants, and removes their memorial from the earth [17].

10.25.3.en: Pride was not created for men, nor the fierceness of wrath for those born of women [18].

10.25.4.en: Man was created in the image of God in meekness and humility. As for the pride that has befallen us, it is from our carelessness and our isolating ourselves from the grace of God.

10.26.s.en: 5. True honor and the fear of the Lord

10.26.0.en: 23 Which seed is honorable? The seed of man. Which seed is honorable? They that fear the Lord. Which seed is base? The seed of man. Which seed is base? They that transgress the commandments. 24 Among brethren their chief is honored, so in the eyes of the Lord are they that fear him. 25 The rich, and the glorious, and the poor, their glory is the fear of the Lord. 26 It is not right to dishonor the wise poor man, nor is it fitting to honor the sinful man. 27 The great, and the judge, and the mighty are honored, and none of them is greater than he that feareth the Lord. 28 The wise servant shall be served by the free, and the prudent man will not murmur.

10.26.1.en: Which kind of seed is honored? The seed of man.

10.26.2.en: Which kind of seed is honored? Those who fear the Lord. Which seed is not honored? The seed of man.

10.26.3.en: Which seed is not honored? Those who transgress the commandments [19].

10.26.4.en: If the fear of the Lord is before man, he enjoys honor by clinging to the Lord, or if before him he transgressed the divine commandment, he brings dishonor upon himself by separation from God. Since Noah feared the Lord (Heb 11:7), he and his household enjoyed deliverance from the Flood, and he even entered into a covenant with God that there would not be a flood to destroy the whole earth.

10.27.0.en: v Distance from keeping the commandments of God is distance from God; and this is the essence of sin, which is separation from God and distance from union with Him [31].

10.27.1.en: St. Basil the Great: The chief among brethren is honored, and those who fear the Lord are honored in His eyes [20].
